implementation_notes: C# has no assert keyword: the facility lives in the BCL as Debug.Assert, which the compiler omits at call sites unless DEBUG is defined because the method carries [Conditional("DEBUG")], and Trace.Assert, which survives into release builds. Rules that callers can violate belong in guards that throw - ArgumentException/ArgumentOutOfRangeException in mutators and ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull in constructors - while Debug.Assert is reserved for states the object's own code should never reach. The former Code Contracts library never shipped in .NET Core, so these BCL mechanisms replace the classic contract structure.
pitfalls: Debug.Assert is compiled away entirely in Release builds: never place a call with side effects in it and never rely on it to protect production data.
Assert shows a modal message box when the process has a UI and a default trace listener; server and CI builds need a listener that throws or writes and fails instead of blocking.
Trace.Assert does run in release, but by default it only writes through TraceListener: without a listener that fails, a violated invariant is merely logged.
Decimal arithmetic can still overflow or round unexpectedly; assert after every mutation rather than only at the end of a long method.
